items.title: What Enterprise Risk Management Is and Why It Matters
items.summary: Enterprise risk management is the framework that helps organisations understand and manage risk across the whole business. This lesson explains why ERM is essential, how it differs from traditional risk management, and how it connects to GRC.
objectives: Define enterprise risk management and distinguish it from traditional risk management
Explain the relationship between risk management, GRC and governance
Describe the key concepts of enterprise risk: risk appetite, inherent risk, residual risk
Describe the role of the GRC professional in enterprise risk management

sections.heading: The problem with traditional risk management
sections.body: Traditional risk management tends to be siloed. Security teams assess security risks, finance teams assess financial risks, HR teams assess people risks, and so on. Each team works in its own silo, produces its own risk register, and reports to its own manager.
bullets: Siloed risk: each department manages its own risks
No enterprise view: no one sees the whole picture
Reactive: risks are addressed after they happen
Inconsistent: different departments use different criteria

sections.heading: What ERM is
sections.body: Enterprise risk management (ERM) is a holistic approach to managing risk across the whole organisation. It is not a department; it is a way of thinking about risk.
bullets: Enterprise: risk is managed across the whole organisation
Holistic: all risks are considered together
Strategic: risk is linked to business objectives
Proactive: risks are identified and managed before they happen

sections.heading: Why ERM matters
sections.body: Organisations face risks that cross traditional boundaries. A cybersecurity breach affects finance, legal, operations, and the board. A supply chain failure affects production, sales, and customers.
bullets: Cyber risk: a breach can bankrupt a company
Operational risk: a factory closure stops revenue
Strategic risk: a market change destroys a business model
Regulatory risk: a missed deadline brings sanctions

sections.heading: GRC is the umbrella
sections.body: GRC (Governance, Risk, and Compliance) is the umbrella under which ERM sits. GRC provides the framework for managing risk, ensuring compliance, and governing the organisation.
bullets: Governance: how the organisation is directed and controlled
Risk: how risks are identified, assessed and managed
Compliance: how the organisation meets its obligations

sections.heading: The risk management framework
sections.body: Most ERM frameworks follow a similar cycle: identify, analyse, evaluate, treat, monitor, communicate.
bullets: Analyse: how likely and how bad?

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: The key concepts of ERM distinguish it from traditional risk management.
bullets: Risk appetite: how much risk is acceptable?
Inherent risk: the risk before controls
Residual risk: the risk after controls
Risk tolerance: the amount of risk you can accept

sections.heading: The GRC professional's role
sections.body: The GRC professional's role in ERM is to connect risk management with governance and compliance. They ensure that risk management is strategic, not just operational.
bullets: Connect risk with strategy: ensure risk management supports business objectives
Connect risk with compliance: ensure regulatory obligations are met
Connect risk with the board: ensure the board understands the risk
Connect risk with controls: ensure controls are effective and efficient

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Write a short paragraph describing the risk management approach you believe a fictional company should take. Identify 5 risks and their treatment.
bullets: Risk 1: Cybersecurity breach - treat with controls
Risk 2: Supply chain disruption - transfer with insurance
Risk 3: Key personnel loss - accept with succession planning
Risk 4: Regulatory change - treat with compliance review
Risk 5: Market change - escalate to the board

practicalExercise.title: Risk appetite statement
practicalExercise.brief: Write a risk appetite statement for a fictional company. Identify 3 risks and state your appetite for each.
steps: Write a risk appetite statement for the company
State your appetite for each risk (high, medium, low)

items.title: ISO 31000 and COSO ERM: The Two Leading ERM Frameworks
items.summary: ISO 31000 and COSO ERM are the two most widely used enterprise risk management frameworks. This lesson compares them, explains their key concepts, and shows how to apply each.
objectives: Explain the structure and philosophy of ISO 31000
Explain the structure and philosophy of COSO ERM
Compare ISO 31000 and COSO ERM
Apply ISO 31000 to a practical risk management scenario

sections.heading: ISO 31000
sections.body: ISO 31000 is the international standard for risk management. It provides the principles, a framework and guidelines for managing risk.
bullets: Principles: the foundation of good risk management
Framework: the structure for building a risk management system
Guidelines: practical guidance on applying the framework

sections.heading: ISO 31000 principles
sections.body: The principles are the foundation of ISO 31000. They describe what good risk management looks like.
bullets: Structured and comprehensive: the framework covers the whole organisation
Tailored: risk management is adapted to the organisation
Includes human and cultural factors: people matter
Embedded: risk management is part of decision-making
Continuously improving: risk management gets better over time

sections.heading: ISO 31000 framework
sections.body: The framework consists of three components: principles, framework and processes.
bullets: Processes: what you do - communication, design, implementation, monitoring, review, improvement

sections.heading: ISO 31000 processes
sections.body: The processes in ISO 31000 are: communication and consultation, establishing the context, risk assessment, and monitoring and review.
bullets: Communication and consultation: talking to stakeholders
Establishing the context: understanding the situation
Risk assessment: identifying, analysing and evaluating risk
Monitoring and review: keeping the risk management current

sections.heading: COSO ERM
sections.body: COSO ERM is the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission's Enterprise Risk Management framework. It is widely used in the US and internationally.
bullets: 8 components: governance and culture, strategy and objective-setting, performance, review and revision, information and communication, risk assessment, risk response, control activities

sections.heading: COSO ERM in practice
sections.body: COSO ERM is structured around eight components. It is practical and widely used.
bullets: Governance: the board and management establish the tone
Strategy: objectives are aligned with risk appetite
Performance: risks are understood and assessed
Review: the risk management system is reviewed
Information: data is provided for decisions
Risk assessment: risks are identified and analysed
Risk response: responses to risks are determined

sections.heading: Comparison
sections.body: Both frameworks have strengths and weaknesses. They are often used together.

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Write a short comparison of ISO 31000 and COSO ERM for a fictional company. Identify which one you would choose and why.
bullets: This company is a small IT services firm (ISO is better)
This company is a large bank with complex regulatory requirements (COSO is better)

practicalExercise.title: Compare ISO 31000 and COSO ERM
practicalExercise.brief: Write a comparison of ISO 31000 and COSO ERM for a fictional company, and identify your preferred choice.

items.title: Risk Identification: Finding the Risks Before They Find You
items.summary: Risk identification is the foundation of enterprise risk management. This lesson covers the tools and techniques for identifying risks across the enterprise.
objectives: List the common sources of enterprise risk
Apply a risk identification workshop format
Categorise risks using a consistent taxonomy
Document risks in a format that feeds the risk register

sections.heading: Why risk identification matters
sections.body: Most risk management failures begin with poorly identified risks. If you do not know what could go wrong, you cannot prepare for it.
bullets: Risks that are not documented cannot be prioritised
Risks that are not communicated cannot be managed

sections.heading: Sources of risk
sections.body: Risks come from many sources across the enterprise.

sections.heading: Risk identification techniques
sections.body: A variety of techniques can be used to find risks.
bullets: Scenario analysis: what if things go wrong?
Cause-and-effect analysis: why does this happen?

sections.heading: Building a risk taxonomy
sections.body: A risk taxonomy is a common way of classifying risks, so that risks from different departments can be compared.
bullets: Sub-categories: business continuity, information security, people, etc.
Taxonomy should reflect the organisation's context

sections.heading: Risk identification workshop
sections.body: A risk identification workshop brings together people from different departments to identify risks.
bullets: Prepare: understand the context, select participants
Document: record risks in a standard format
Review: check the output before it goes to the risk register

sections.heading: Risk identification in practice
sections.body: A risk register is the output of the risk identification process. It records each risk, its owner and its status.
bullets: Risk description: what could go wrong?
Current controls: what are you doing?

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Run a risk identification exercise for a fictional company. Identify at least 10 risks and document them in a risk register format.

practicalExercise.title: Risk identification workshop
practicalExercise.brief: Run a risk identification exercise for a fictional company. Identify at least 10 risks and document them.
steps: Select the department or risk domain
practicalExercise.deliverable: A risk register with at least 10 risks.

items.title: Risk Analysis: Likelihood, Impact and Scoring
items.summary: Risk analysis is the process of estimating the likelihood and impact of a risk. This lesson covers scoring methods, risk matrices and how to interpret them.
objectives: Explain the difference between likelihood and impact
Describe common scoring scales for likelihood and impact
Apply a 5x5 risk matrix to assess risks
Interpret risk ratings and determine treatment priorities

sections.heading: What risk analysis is
sections.body: Risk analysis determines the level of risk. It involves two steps: estimating likelihood and estimating impact.
bullets: Likelihood: how likely is the risk to happen?
Impact: how bad would it be if it happened?

sections.heading: Likelihood
sections.body: Likelihood is the probability of a risk occurring in a given time period.
bullets: Expressed as a score or percentage
Should be based on data where possible
Should be consistent across the organisation

sections.heading: Impact
sections.body: Impact is the consequence of the risk occurring.

sections.heading: Scoring scales
sections.body: A scoring scale is used to convert likelihood and impact into numbers.

sections.heading: Risk matrix
sections.body: The risk matrix combines likelihood and impact into a risk rating.
bullets: Each cell has a risk rating
Ratings can be Low, Medium, High, Extreme
The matrix is used to prioritise risks

sections.heading: Risk ratings
sections.body: Risk ratings determine how you respond to risks.
bullets: Medium: action required within agreed timeframe
High: action required urgently, escalate to management
Extreme: immediate action required, urgent escalation

sections.heading: Consistency
sections.body: Consistency in scoring is critical for comparing risks.
bullets: Use the same scale across the organisation

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Score 5 risks for a fictional company using a 5x5 matrix. Calculate the risk rating for each.
bullets: Risk 1: Customer data breach - likelihood 4, impact 5
Risk 2: Key staff leaving - likelihood 3, impact 4

practicalExercise.title: Risk scoring exercise
practicalExercise.brief: Score 5 risks for a fictional company using a 5x5 matrix and calculate risk ratings.

items.title: Risk Treatment: Accept, Treat, Avoid, Transfer or Escalate
items.summary: Once risks are identified and scored, the organisation must decide what to do about them. This lesson covers risk treatment options and how to evaluate their effectiveness.
objectives: Explain the four risk treatment options: accept, treat, avoid, transfer
Describe when each treatment option is appropriate
Write a risk treatment plan
Explain how to evaluate the effectiveness of risk treatments

sections.heading: The risk treatment decision
sections.body: Once a risk is assessed, the organisation must decide what to do about it. The four treatment options are: accept, treat, avoid and transfer.
bullets: Accept: the risk is within risk appetite
Treat: apply controls to reduce the risk
Avoid: change the plan to remove the risk
Transfer: share the risk with another party

sections.heading: Accept
sections.body: Accepting a risk means acknowledging it and continuing with business as usual.

sections.heading: Treat
sections.body: Treating a risk means applying controls to reduce its likelihood or impact.
bullets: Apply controls to reduce likelihood or impact

sections.heading: Avoid
sections.body: Avoiding a risk means changing the plan to remove the risk.
bullets: Avoiding is the most powerful option

sections.heading: Transfer
sections.body: Transferring a risk means sharing it with another party.

sections.heading: Risk treatment plan
sections.body: A risk treatment plan records what will be done about each risk.
bullets: Target date: when will it be done?

sections.heading: Evaluating treatment effectiveness
sections.body: After controls are applied, the organisation must evaluate whether they are working.
bullets: Review: has the risk been reduced?
Reassess: is the risk still acceptable?
Adjust: do you need to change direction?

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: For a fictional company, write a risk treatment plan for 5 risks. Include treatment, owner, target date and expected outcome.
bullets: Risk 1: Customer data breach - treat with controls
Risk 3: Supply chain disruption - transfer with insurance
Risk 4: Key person departure - avoid with succession planning

practicalExercise.title: Risk treatment plan
practicalExercise.brief: Write a risk treatment plan for a fictional company covering 5 risks.

items.title: The Enterprise Risk Register: Your Single Source of Truth
items.summary: The risk register is the central document of enterprise risk management. This lesson covers its structure, how to maintain it, and how to use it for decision-making.
objectives: Explain the structure and purpose of the risk register
Build a risk register from a set of risks
Explain how the risk register is used for prioritisation
Describe how the risk register is used in reporting

sections.heading: What the risk register is
sections.body: The risk register is the single document that records all the risks facing the organisation, their status, and the actions being taken.
bullets: Central repository: one place for all risks
Accountability: each risk has an owner
Prioritisation: risks are ranked by severity

sections.heading: Structure of the risk register
sections.body: A risk register should contain enough information to manage the risk, but not so much that it becomes a burden.
bullets: Risk description: what could go wrong?
Risk rating: what is the priority?
Current controls: what are you doing?
Target date: when is it done?

sections.heading: Using the risk register
sections.body: The risk register is used for several purposes.
bullets: Prioritisation: which risks need attention first?

sections.heading: Risk register maintenance
sections.body: The risk register is a living document. It must be kept up to date.
bullets: Archive: close old risks, update new ones

sections.heading: Reporting from the risk register
sections.body: The risk register provides the data for risk reporting.
bullets: Trend analysis: are risks getting better or worse?
Summary: high-level view for the board
Detail: operational view for risk owners

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Build a risk register for a fictional company. Include at least 5 risks with all the standard fields.
bullets: Risk 1: Customer data breach - High risk, treat
Risk 2: Ransomware - Extreme risk, treat heavily
Risk 3: Key staff loss - Medium risk, accept with monitoring

practicalExercise.title: Risk register build
practicalExercise.brief: Build a risk register for a fictional company with at least 5 risks.
steps: Record the risk owner and target date

items.title: KRI, KPIs and Dashboards: Measuring Risk in the Enterprise
items.summary: Key risk indicators (KRIs) and key performance indicators (KPIs) provide the metrics that tell you whether your risk management is working. This lesson explains how to design and use them.
objectives: Explain the difference between KPIs and KRIs
Design KRIs for a fictional company
Describe how to interpret and act on KRIs
Describe how risk dashboards are used by boards and management

sections.heading: KPIs vs KRIs
sections.body: KPIs and KRIs are different. They measure different things.
bullets: KPIs: are we achieving our objectives?
KRIs: is our risk management working?

sections.heading: What makes a good KRI
sections.body: A good KRI is measurable, relevant, and leads to action.

sections.heading: Designing KRIs
sections.body: Designing KRIs is the process of identifying the metrics your organisation needs.
bullets: Determine what would indicate the risk is increasing

sections.heading: Responding to KRIs
sections.body: A KRI without action is just data. You must do something with it.

sections.heading: Risk dashboards
sections.body: Risk dashboards present KRI and KPI data in a visual format for boards and management.
bullets: Trend view: how are risks changing?

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Design 5 KRIs for a fictional company. Include the definition, threshold, owner, and response trigger.
bullets: KRI 2: % of critical systems backed up
KRI 3: % of employees trained on security

practicalExercise.title: Design KRIs for a fictional company
practicalExercise.brief: Design 5 KRIs for a fictional company. Include definition, threshold, owner, and response trigger.

items.title: Emerging Risks: Cyber, AI, Geopolitics and the Uncertain Future
items.summary: Emerging risks are risks that are not yet fully understood or established. This lesson covers how to identify and manage emerging risks including cyber, AI, climate and geopolitical risk.
objectives: Explain what an emerging risk is and how it differs from a known risk
Identify emerging risks relevant to 2026 (cyber, AI, climate, geopolitical)
Apply horizon scanning to identify emerging risks
Describe how to manage risk without historical data

sections.heading: What is an emerging risk?
sections.body: Emerging risks are risks that are not yet fully understood or established. They may be new, or they may be existing risks that are changing rapidly.

sections.heading: Cyber risk is always emerging
sections.body: Cyber threats change constantly. What was emerging five years ago is now common.
bullets: Ransomware is increasingly targeted and disruptive
Supply chain attacks attacking through suppliers
AI-augmented attacks using AI to find vulnerabilities

sections.heading: AI risk is emerging
sections.body: Artificial intelligence introduces new risk categories.
bullets: AI model risk: models producing biased or incorrect outputs
Data leakage: sensitive data fed into AI systems
Shadow AI: using AI without governance
AI third-party risk: AI vendors may be unvetted

sections.heading: Climate and geopolitical risk
sections.body: Climate and geopolitical risks are becoming more prominent.
bullets: Climate: physical risks (floods, heat) and transition risks (regulation, market)
Geopolitical: war, sanctions, supply chain disruption
Regulatory: new laws impacting technology and data

sections.heading: Horizon scanning
sections.body: Horizon scanning is the process of looking for risks before they become mainstream.
bullets: Get the signals: media, research, conversations
Assess: could this become a risk?
Act: is there anything to do?

sections.heading: Managing unknown risks
sections.body: Without historical data, you cannot use standard risk assessment techniques. You must use judgement.
bullets: Pre-mortems: imagine the failure before it happens
Robustness: build systems that can absorb shocks

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Write a short risk horizon scan for a fictional company covering the next 12 months. Identify 5 emerging risks.

practicalExercise.title: Horizon scan for emerging risks
practicalExercise.brief: Write a short risk horizon scan covering the next 12 months for a fictional company.

items.title: Risk Governance: Who Owns Risk and How Decisions Are Made
items.summary: Risk governance is about who decides, who is accountable, and how risk decisions are made. This lesson covers governance structures, board reporting, and the relationship between management and the board.
objectives: Describe the roles and responsibilities in risk governance
Explain how risk decisions are made at board level
Design a risk governance framework for a fictional organisation
Describe how risk reporting should be structured for different audiences

sections.heading: Risk governance structure
sections.body: Risk governance is the framework of roles and responsibilities for risk management.
bullets: Risk ownership: operational ownership of risks

sections.heading: The board's role
sections.body: The board provides ultimate accountability for risk.

sections.heading: Management's role
sections.body: Management implements the risk framework.
bullets: Monitors risks and reports to the board
Decides on risk responses within risk appetite

sections.heading: Risk appetite
sections.body: Risk appetite is the amount of risk an organisation is willing to accept.
bullets: Risk appetite statement: what risks can you take?
Risk tolerance: specific limits on risk
Risk threshold: the trigger for escalation

sections.heading: Board reporting
sections.body: Risk reporting must match the board's needs.
bullets: Clear and concise: not too detailed

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Design a risk governance structure for a fictional company. Include board roles, management roles, and risk owner responsibilities.
bullets: Board: risk appetite approved, regular reporting

practicalExercise.title: Design a risk governance framework
practicalExercise.brief: Design a risk governance structure for a fictional company.

items.title: Risk Quantification: FAIR, ALE and Cyber Risk Expressions
items.summary: Risk quantification puts numbers on risk so that boards and management can make decisions. This lesson covers FAIR fundamentals, Annualized Loss Expectancy, and how to express cyber risk in business terms.
objectives: Explain the difference between qualitative and quantitative risk assessment
Describe the FAIR risk analysis fundamentals
Calculate Annualized Loss Expectancy (ALE)
Express cyber risk in financial terms for executive reporting

sections.heading: Qualitative vs quantitative
sections.body: Qualitative risk assessment uses words (Low, Medium, High). Quantitative risk assessment uses numbers. Both have their place.
bullets: Many organisations start qualitative and move to quantitative

sections.heading: FAIR fundamentals
sections.body: FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) is the international standard for quantitative information risk analysis.
bullets: Loss event frequency: how often will loss occur?
Loss magnitude: how much will it cost?
Primary loss: direct cost to the organisation
Secondary loss: cost to others affected

sections.heading: ALE calculation
sections.body: Annualized Loss Expectancy (ALE) = Single Loss Expectancy (SLE) × Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO).
bullets: SLE: cost of one loss event
sections.callout: ALE helps you decide whether a control is worth its cost.

sections.heading: Expressing cyber risk in financial terms
sections.body: Boards understand money, not technical risk ratings. Express cyber risk in dollars, rupees, pounds or euros.
bullets: Translate technical risk to financial impact
Compare control cost to expected loss

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Calculate ALE for three risks for a fictional company.
bullets: Risk 1: Data breach - SLE: $500,000, ARO: 0.1, ALE: $50,000
Risk 2: System downtime - SLE: $100,000, ARO: 2, ALE: $200,000
Risk 3: Insider theft - SLE: $200,000, ARO: 0.5, ALE: $100,000

practicalExercise.title: ALE calculation exercise
practicalExercise.brief: Calculate ALE for three risks for a fictional company.

items.title: Third-Party Risk Management in the Enterprise
items.summary: Third-party risk is the risk that comes from your suppliers, vendors and partners. This lesson covers vendor onboarding, due diligence, risk scoring and continuous monitoring.
objectives: Explain why third-party risk matters to the enterprise
Describe vendor classification and due diligence
Apply vendor risk scoring
Design right-to-audit clauses and SLAs

sections.heading: Why third-party risk matters
sections.body: Organisations do not operate alone. Suppliers, vendors, cloud providers and partners all access data and systems. A failure at a vendor can become a failure at your organisation.

sections.heading: Vendor classification
sections.body: Not all vendors are equal. Classify vendors by their access to data and systems.
bullets: Critical: access to customer data or critical systems

sections.heading: Due diligence
sections.body: Before onboarding a vendor, perform due diligence.

sections.heading: Vendor risk scoring
sections.body: Score each vendor to prioritise oversight.

sections.heading: Contractual protections
sections.body: Contracts are your primary tool for managing vendor risk.

sections.heading: Continuous monitoring
sections.body: Vendor risk changes over time. Monitor continuously.

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Classify 5 vendors for a fictional company and assign risk ratings.
bullets: Vendor 1: Cloud provider - Critical, High risk
Vendor 2: Payroll processor - High, High risk
Vendor 3: Office supplies - Low, Low risk

practicalExercise.title: Vendor classification and risk scoring
practicalExercise.brief: Classify 5 vendors for a fictional company and assign risk ratings.

items.title: Business Continuity Risk and the BIA
items.summary: Business continuity risk is the risk that your organisation cannot operate after a disruption. This lesson covers BIA, RTO, RPO, MTPD and continuity strategies.
objectives: Explain BIA, RTO, RPO and MTPD
Describe business continuity strategies
Explain the relationship between ERM and business continuity
Build a simple BIA for a fictional organisation

sections.heading: What is business continuity risk?
sections.body: Business continuity risk is the risk that a disruption prevents your organisation from delivering products or services.

sections.heading: BIA fundamentals
sections.body: Business Impact Analysis (BIA) identifies critical business functions and the impact of losing them.
bullets: Critical functions: what must keep running?
Impact over time: what happens after 1 hour, 4 hours, 24 hours?
Dependencies: what systems, people and suppliers support each function?

sections.heading: RTO, RPO and MTPD
sections.body: These are the key metrics of business continuity.
bullets: RTO: Recovery Time Objective - how quickly must you recover?
RPO: Recovery Point Objective - how much data can you lose?
MTPD: Maximum Tolerable Period of Disruption - how long can you be down?

sections.heading: Continuity strategies
sections.body: Strategies for keeping the organisation running.
bullets: Hot site: fully operational backup site
Warm site: partially equipped backup site
Cold site: empty space with infrastructure
Reciprocal agreement: mutual aid with another organisation

sections.heading: ERM and business continuity
sections.body: Business continuity is part of ERM. Continuity risks are enterprise risks.
bullets: BCP is part of the risk register

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Build a simple BIA for a fictional company with 3 critical functions.
bullets: Function 1: Online banking - RTO: 4 hours, RPO: 1 hour
Function 2: Payroll - RTO: 24 hours, RPO: 24 hours
Function 3: Customer support - RTO: 8 hours, RPO: 4 hours

practicalExercise.title: Simple BIA for a fictional company
practicalExercise.brief: Build a BIA for a fictional company with 3 critical functions.
steps: Determine RTO and RPO for each
